segments.text: This is a mathematics scratchpad. The working on screen is real, and half finished. It has never been submitted anywhere, so no server has ever seen it. An agent has just asked the page to check it, and the page has marked the first line that stopped being true. Line three. Nothing after it is marked, because everything after it follows from a mistake.
That verdict did not come from a language model. It came from a computer algebra system running inside the page, and the badge you are looking at is rendered from its return value.
This is the whole WebMCP surface. Eighteen tools, nine that read and nine that write, grouped so that an agent, or a person, can see its shape and its size without clicking anything.

These four are the interesting ones. An agent can differentiate, evaluate, and compare expressions against the page's own engine before it writes anything to a learner's work. Every agent we pointed at this page used them unprompted.

Now the agent repairs the line it broke, and asks the page to check again. It can do that. This page used to refuse every agent write, and we withdrew the refusal, because a permission check in our own code never bound anything outside this page.
Every line is sound. What replaces the refusal is attribution: the receipt records who wrote each line, and says so even when the answer is that an agent wrote all of them.

And this is the part we are proudest of. Every one of these seven verdicts was produced by executing the feature in your browser, just now. Three work. Two, origin scoping and cross origin reads, Chrome accepts and silently does not honour. One more is absent altogether. A page that believed origin scoping worked would be shipping a security assumption the browser does not implement. So we publish what the platform does not do, alongside what it does.
